title: NFT BOT for Mint on Sailor (Front Running Bot) | NFT Mint Bot
description: In this video, I show my script - a bot that allows NFT to mint on the sailor, sending advanced transactions, the Ethereum Mempool monitor, as I showed you in one of the previous videos and carrying out Front Running. Link to the script (after shooting the video, a check was also added which method we twitch):  https://github.com/bedrosovayulia/ethereumpendingtransactionchecker/blob/master/buy_nft_bot.js  Video on how to monitor Ethereum Mempool: https://youtu.be/aiwzegsadhc

asr.full_text: Hello everyone! Hi, Julia Bedrosov. We're going to continue to discuss the topic of front-end. And today I'm going to show you how you can use front-end to buy some valuable NFT on the payline. Which you might not get if you try to buy it with your hands. So now I'm going to show you a simple NFT-buying bot that will buy it with Chrome Training attack. As usual in a video of this disclaimer that's salting all their money with this script, I'm not going to answer for anything. Now let's see the code itself. And this bot, which I wrote for educational purposes, with the most basic functionality, based on the mempu monitoring script I showed you in one of the previous videos, it works like this. When a sequel starts and a lot of people are sitting on the sequel's website, they update a page, they plug in their wallet and wait for the buy button. So I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to double the price of gas. I'm going to sign a new transaction with my key. And you also have to keep in mind that if you look at my script algorithm, you'll see that it's going to buy until you either stop the script or you run out of money in your account. I didn't put any restrictions on it, so the account you're going to buy from is going to put as much money as you need to buy NFT, plus more, then, money for gas. So let's check it out. Let's check it out right now on OpenSea. I already bought one NFT chip from this valuable collection I want to buy on this fourth account. Now, it turns out we're going to run our script. I run it. It starts the transactions. So we're going to verify the accounts on this site. It doesn't matter if the account is verified or not. I'm going to go to his account right here. And I'm going to buy an NFT from the address of the person who is actually sitting and buying it with his hands. And the only way I'm going to get this right now is to put the price of gas down here because I only monitor the transaction pool once every five seconds. And in real life, if you're going to do this, you just have to check the transaction more often. I think that once a second that's going to be too rare. And actually, now our script went to that transaction and it has to send our second fake transaction. So we're going to see that we have a new NFT from this collection. And look, we got 40 NFTs, and we get 41, the first, 40 NFTs, they're still being received by the person who sent the transaction first. So we sent a little gas in our transaction. So let's increase the gas limit. Let's try again. I run our script. I go to the site from the account of the person who will buy the hand. I connect here. I do the Bye. But the only thing you can see, of course, is that we overpaid for gas from this fourth account very seriously. Actually, we only spent 0.005 of our air on gas for our experiments. And then, going to the address of the contract we had all the time, we can also check that the transaction was the first one. I'm going to put it in a separate brunch room in the same repository that I put the previous script on this topic in. And I'm going to leave a link in the description to this video.

textual.observation: The video demonstrates a bot that monitors pending NFT transactions, raises gas price, and submits a transaction intended to acquire an NFT before a person who is manually buying it.

evidence.quote: a bot that allows NFT to mint on the sailor, sending advanced transactions, the Ethereum Mempool monitor
I'm going to double the price of gas.
I'm going to buy an NFT from the address of the person who is actually sitting and buying it with his hands.

textual.context: Presented as a coding demonstration or educational video; the source does not establish whether the described transaction behavior violates any rule or agreement.
textual.potential_relevance: The demonstrated bot links a requested transaction and increased gas payment to obtaining an NFT ahead of another buyer, making the transaction-ordering mechanism relevant for later assessment.
textual.limitations: The records do not establish actual harm, loss, rule violations, ownership, transaction validity, or whether the demonstration was performed on a live transaction.

textual.observation: The script is described as continuing NFT purchases until stopped or until the account runs out of money, without configured spending restrictions, and requiring funds for NFT purchases and gas.

I didn't put any restrictions on it
the account you're going to buy from is going to put as much money as you need to buy NFT, plus more, then, money for gas.

textual.context: This is a stated property of the demonstrated script, with no indication in the supplied records that viewers are being promised a return or that losses occurred.
textual.potential_relevance: An unrestricted automated purchase loop is linked to the requested funding of an account for NFT and gas payments, creating a concrete money-flow and spending-control cue for later review.
textual.limitations: The records do not establish that viewers were asked to fund an account, that any funds were lost, or the actual limits or safeguards of the code.

visual.observation: A code editor shows a JavaScript script named like a transaction checker that subscribes to pending transactions, reads a transaction by hash, checks whether the transaction target matches a configured contract address, then constructs and signs a new transaction to the same target with the same value and a higher gas price before sending it.
visual.context: The visible context is a coding demonstration or development session; no spoken explanation is available in the sampled frames.
visual.potential_relevance: The observed relationship is a mechanism that monitors pending blockchain transactions and submits a competing signed transaction with increased gas price to the same contract, which conditionally merits review as an explicit transaction-prioritization/bypass-style workflow rather than a routine crypto mention alone.
visual.limitations: The frames do not establish intent, whether this was used on a live network, whether any third party was affected, or whether the code successfully bypassed any rule; some code details and addresses are only partially legible.

visual.observation: A browser page for “BAD CRYPTO TEENS” displays an NFT mint interface showing “39 / 1000,” “1 BCT costs 0.05 ETH,” “Excluding gas fees,” “Click buy to mint your NFT,” and a visible “BUY” button.
visual.context: The page appears to be an NFT minting site shown during the same sequence as wallet and coding screens; the context is unclear beyond a demonstration/development workflow.
visual.potential_relevance: The observed relationship is a requested mint/purchase action linked to a stated crypto payment amount and gas fees, and it is shown alongside the transaction-monitoring script, making the payment/action flow relevant to review in this specific sequence.
visual.limitations: An NFT price and buy button alone are routine commercial content; the frames do not show a completed purchase from this page, prove ownership value, or establish that the site is deceptive.

visual.observation: A MetaMask wallet panel on Rinkeby Test Network is visible over the NFT mint page, showing account balances and account selection while the mint page remains in the background.
visual.context: The wallet appears to be part of a testnet interaction with the mint page; no prompt requesting sensitive information is visible.
visual.potential_relevance: The observed relationship is a crypto wallet being used in connection with an NFT mint interface that requests payment, providing visible payment/account-flow context for the transaction demonstration.
visual.limitations: The frames do not show seed phrase entry, permission approval, a confirmed wallet signature prompt, or any real-money transfer.

visual.observation: Later frames show OpenSea Testnet details for a minted ERC-721 token and an Etherscan Rinkeby transaction details page with successful status and token transfer information, while MetaMask shows a reduced RinkebyETH balance.
visual.context: These are testnet explorer/marketplace views following the minting and code demonstration sequence.
visual.potential_relevance: The observed relationship is that the demonstrated mint/payment flow is followed by visible testnet transaction and minted-token records, which may help contextualize whether the earlier transaction-monitoring code was being demonstrated against a mint contract.
visual.limitations: The frames only show testnet pages and cannot establish real financial impact, verify the transaction externally, or prove causation from any specific user action between sampled frames.

The sequence alternates between a local code editor/terminal and browser-based NFT, wallet, marketplace, and block-explorer pages.

annotation.contextual_rationale: The video presents a concrete mechanism for monitoring pending NFT transactions and submitting a competing purchase with a higher gas price, including a stated relationship to another person's manual purchase, which supports interpreting the demonstrated transaction-ordering workflow as scam-relevant. The associated mint page requests a 0.05 ETH payment plus gas through a BUY action, while the later visible transaction record is explicitly on Rinkeby Testnet and therefore documents a demonstrated testnet payment flow rather than established real-world financial loss. The educational framing is material counterevidence against inferring creator endorsement or malicious intent, and the supplied records do not establish that viewers were solicited, that a live-network victim was affected, or that the mechanism caused a completed theft.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary mechanism is an explicit front-running or transaction-ordering workflow: the bot monitors pending NFT transactions, raises the gas price, and submits a competing NFT purchase associated with another person's manual purchase. This is a presented mechanism for obtaining an asset through transaction prioritization; the evidence does not establish successful exploitation on a live network.
